column1: Start a protected T-SQL block with {{c1::BEGIN TRY}}.
column2:
Put statements that can fail inside TRY. A catchable error transfers control to the associated handler.
BEGIN TRY
    SELECT 1 / 0 AS Result;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    SELECT ERROR_NUMBER() AS ErrorNumber, ERROR_MESSAGE() AS ErrorMessage;
    THROW;
END CATCH;
Review source

column1: END TRY must be followed immediately by {{c1::BEGIN CATCH}}.
column2:
CATCH must be immediately paired with TRY. A statement inserted between them breaks the construct.
BEGIN TRY
    SELECT 1 / 0 AS Result;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    SELECT ERROR_NUMBER() AS ErrorNumber, ERROR_MESSAGE() AS ErrorMessage;
    THROW;
END CATCH;
Review source

column1: A TRY...CATCH construct must remain within one {{c1::batch}}.
column2:
GO separates batches in client tools. It cannot divide the TRY block from its CATCH.
Review source

column1: Within CATCH, {{c1::ERROR_NUMBER()}} returns the caught error's numeric identifier.
column2:
The number lets a caller distinguish errors such as a duplicate key from unrelated failures.
BEGIN TRY
    SELECT 1 / 0;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    SELECT ERROR_NUMBER() AS ErrorDetail;
END CATCH;
Review source

column1: Within CATCH, {{c1::ERROR_MESSAGE()}} returns the complete error message text.
column2:
Read this value for the human-readable details. Use ERROR_NUMBER when logic needs a stable numeric identifier.
BEGIN TRY
    SELECT 1 / 0;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    SELECT ERROR_MESSAGE() AS ErrorDetail;
END CATCH;
Review source

column1: Within CATCH, {{c1::ERROR_SEVERITY()}} returns the caught error's severity level.
column2:
Severity describes the level of the error. The state instead helps distinguish where a particular error was raised.
BEGIN TRY
    SELECT 1 / 0;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    SELECT ERROR_SEVERITY() AS ErrorDetail;
END CATCH;
Review source

column1: Within CATCH, {{c1::ERROR_STATE()}} returns the caught error's state number.
column2:
Two checks can share an error number while using different state values. That helps locate the failing branch.
BEGIN TRY
    SELECT 1 / 0;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    SELECT ERROR_STATE() AS ErrorDetail;
END CATCH;
Review source

column1: Within CATCH, {{c1::ERROR_LINE()}} returns the line where the error occurred.
column2:
The value points to the failing code, not to the line that calls ERROR_LINE in the handler.
BEGIN TRY
    SELECT 1 / 0;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    SELECT ERROR_LINE() AS ErrorDetail;
END CATCH;
Review source

column1: Within CATCH, {{c1::ERROR_PROCEDURE()}} returns the name of the stored procedure or trigger where the error originated.
column2:
The result names the stored procedure or trigger of origin. An error in an ad hoc batch need not have an object name.
BEGIN TRY
    SELECT 1 / 0;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    SELECT ERROR_PROCEDURE() AS ErrorDetail;
END CATCH;
Review source

column1: Outside the scope of any CATCH, the ERROR_* information functions return {{c1::NULL}}.
column2:
These functions report an error only within a CATCH context. They are not a general history of prior failures.
SELECT ERROR_NUMBER() AS ErrorNumber,
       ERROR_MESSAGE() AS ErrorMessage;
-- Outside CATCH, both are NULL.
Review source

column1: Inside CATCH, rethrow the caught exception with {{c1::THROW;}}.
column2:
The argumentless form sends the same exception onward. Handle cleanup first because later statements do not run.
BEGIN TRY
    SELECT 1 / 0 AS Result;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    SELECT ERROR_NUMBER() AS ErrorNumber, ERROR_MESSAGE() AS ErrorMessage;
    THROW;
END CATCH;
Review source

column1: If a caught error has severity 14, bare THROW; rethrows it with severity {{c1::14}}.
column2:
Severity 16 applies when THROW creates a new error, not when it forwards an existing one.
Review source

column1: A newly numbered THROW requires an error number of at least {{c1::50000}}.
column2:
A new error number must be in the user-defined range. An argumentless rethrow can preserve a smaller system number.
THROW 50001, N'Invalid quantity.', 7;
-- Number: 50001, message: Invalid quantity., state: 7
Review source

column1: THROW accepts state values from {{c1::0 to 255}}.
column2:
The state identifies a raise site if you choose to use it that way. It is not the error severity.
THROW 50001, N'Invalid quantity.', 7;
-- Number: 50001, message: Invalid quantity., state: 7
Review source

column1: A THROW that initiates a new exception sets severity to {{c1::16}}.
column2:
The new-error form has number, message, and state. SQL Server supplies severity 16.
THROW 50001, N'Invalid quantity.', 7;
-- Number: 50001, message: Invalid quantity., state: 7
Review source

column1: In THROW 50001, N'Invalid quantity.', 7; the 7 is the {{c1::state}}.
column2:
This state can identify the validation branch without choosing a different error number.
THROW 50001, N'Invalid quantity.', 7;
-- Number: 50001, message: Invalid quantity., state: 7
Review source

column1: The statement immediately before THROW must end with {{c1::a semicolon (;)}}.
column2:
End the previous statement so THROW starts separately. This requirement applies to a new error and a rethrow.
BEGIN TRY
    SELECT 1 / 0 AS Result;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    SELECT ERROR_NUMBER() AS ErrorNumber, ERROR_MESSAGE() AS ErrorMessage;
    THROW;
END CATCH;
Review source

column1: For new T-SQL error-raising code, Microsoft recommends {{c1::THROW}}.
column2:
THROW honors SET XACT_ABORT. Use it without arguments in CATCH when the caller needs the original error.
Review source

column1: In a RAISERROR message, %s substitutes a {{c1::string}}.
column2:
For example, substitute a table name into a message containing %s. The parameter is message text, not the severity.
RAISERROR(N'Invalid table: %s.', 16, 1, N'Orders');
Review source

column1: In a RAISERROR message, %d formats a {{c1::signed integer}}.
column2:
The substitution inserts a signed decimal integer into the formatted message. It does not replace the error's number.
RAISERROR(N'Invalid quantity: %d.', 16, 1, 0);
Review source

column1: Enable automatic transaction abort for applicable run-time errors with SET {{c1::XACT_ABORT}} ON;
column2:
Use CATCH to inspect the resulting transaction state. The option does not cover compilation or make RAISERROR honor it.
SET XACT_ABORT ON;
BEGIN TRY
    BEGIN TRANSACTION;
    UPDATE dbo.Orders SET Status = 'Ready' WHERE OrderID = 1;
    COMMIT TRANSACTION;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    IF XACT_STATE() <> 0 ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;
    THROW;
END CATCH;
Review source

column1: XACT_STATE() = {{c1::0}} means there is no active user transaction.
column2:
Zero means there is no user transaction to clean up. A handler can still report or rethrow the error.
SELECT XACT_STATE() AS TransactionState; -- 0 when no user transaction is active
Review source

column1: XACT_STATE() = {{c1::1}} means the active user transaction is committable.
column2:
One means SQL Server permits COMMIT. It does not mean the application should commit incomplete work.
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
SELECT XACT_STATE() AS TransactionState; -- 1
ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;
Review source

column1: XACT_STATE() = {{c1::-1}} means the active user transaction cannot be committed.
column2:
With a doomed transaction, an ordinary write or commit cannot succeed. Roll back the entire transaction before writing.
SET XACT_ABORT ON;
BEGIN TRY
    BEGIN TRANSACTION;
    SELECT CAST('invalid' AS int);
    COMMIT TRANSACTION;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    SELECT XACT_STATE() AS TransactionState; -- -1
    IF XACT_STATE() <> 0 ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;
    THROW;
END CATCH;
Review source

column1: Start an explicit transaction with {{c1::BEGIN TRANSACTION}};
column2:
The transaction can cover multiple statements. A bare BEGIN...END block does not start one.
SET XACT_ABORT ON;
BEGIN TRY
    BEGIN TRANSACTION;
    UPDATE dbo.Orders SET Status = 'Ready' WHERE OrderID = 1;
    COMMIT TRANSACTION;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    IF XACT_STATE() <> 0 ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;
    THROW;
END CATCH;
Review source

column1: For a transaction your procedure owns, IF {{c1::@@TRANCOUNT}} > 0 ROLLBACK TRANSACTION; avoids rollback when none is active.
column2:
Use this guard for a transaction the procedure owns. A positive count is not permission to commit.
SET XACT_ABORT ON;
BEGIN TRY
    BEGIN TRANSACTION;
    UPDATE dbo.Orders SET Status = 'Ready' WHERE OrderID = 1;
    COMMIT TRANSACTION;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    IF XACT_STATE() <> 0 ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;
    THROW;
END CATCH;
Review source

column1: A successful COMMIT TRANSACTION changes @@TRANCOUNT from 2 to {{c1::1}}.
column2:
The inner commit lowers the nesting count only. Work is not committed until the outer transaction commits.
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
COMMIT TRANSACTION;
SELECT @@TRANCOUNT AS RemainingCount; -- 1
ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;
Review source

column1: In RAISERROR(N'Invalid quantity.', 16, 1), 16 is the {{c1::severity}}.
column2:
A severity of 16 can send control from TRY to CATCH. The final state value is a different field.
RAISERROR(N'Invalid quantity: %d.', 16, 1, 0);
Review source
